extracted.intended_audience: administrative law scholars, policymakers, agency officials, and engaged citizens/advocates
extracted.subtask_description: Producing effective public comments on administrative rulemakings—comments that engage agency reasoning, statutory authority, and underlying empirical analyses so they can influence agency decisions or preserve issues for review. Also includes implications for agencies seeking to increase meaningful citizen participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: High technical/regulatory literacy required
rubrics_metrics.description: The bar to writing an 'effective' comment is high - requires technical/regulatory literacy. Cognitive and motivational barriers are the more significant obstacles to citizen participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical findings show e-rulemaking alone makes little difference; commenters need substantive knowledge to understand and engage with rulemakings. Plain lowering of technological barriers will not by itself democratize participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding of the specific statutory authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Real participation requires understanding of the specific statutory authority for the rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments should demonstrate knowledge of the enabling statute and the scope of agency authority to frame objections or suggestions within legal bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engagement with the agency's prior reasoning (preamble)
rubrics_metrics.description: Real participation requires understanding of the agency's prior reasoning in the preamble.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective comments reference, critique, or build on the agency's stated reasoning in the rule's preamble rather than addressing the rule in isolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address economic and scientific analyses (RIA, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Real participation requires understanding of the economic and scientific analyses (Regulatory Impact Analyses and similar studies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments should engage with, challenge, or supply alternative empirical and analytic evidence (e.g., RIAs, scientific studies) rather than relying solely on unsupported assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awareness of legal and procedural standards for judicial review
rubrics_metrics.description: Real participation requires understanding of the legal/procedural standards for judicial review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters should frame arguments to preserve issues for potential litigation and to align with standards courts use when reviewing agency action (e.g., reasoned decisionmaking, record support).

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive thoughtfulness differentiates comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Most rulemakings receive few comments - a thoughtful comment can stand out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid boilerplate or purely expressive submissions; provide concrete analysis, specific alternatives, or targeted data to increase the likelihood of influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technological facilitation alone is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Lowering technological barriers alone does not democratize participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because cognitive and motivational barriers remain dominant, solutions must go beyond e-rulemaking tools—address outreach, education, and incentives for substantive engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency responsibility to seek earlier and improved public participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should do a better job of seeking citizen comment earlier in the rulemaking process and improve transparency and public participation procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendations from a task force include procedural reforms to solicit input before formal rule proposals (early engagement), which can help mitigate barriers and improve the substance of public participation.
